texts.value: Read the route
By the end of this lesson, you can identify a station on the route sketch and distinguish a station name from a signal instruction.

Lantern Marsh is an invented place. Its keepers carry coloured shutters between reed islands. Tonight you join keeper Mira on the west route. The stations are Sedge Gate, Moth Bend and Last Reed. A name tells you where a record belongs. A signal tells the next keeper what happened there.
The route ledger stays at Sedge Gate. Write the station name before adding a signal.
route ledger
The shared notebook that records station visits in route order.
Follow the sketch
Start at Sedge Gate and follow the boardwalk to Moth Bend. Last Reed sits beyond the fork. The dotted line is a return path used when the low boardwalk closes.
The three stations on the west route.

texts.value: Three shutter states
By the end of this lesson, you can interpret the clear and hold shutter states and explain when to leave a shutter covered.

The station lantern has a clear opening and an amber shutter. Clear means the next station may send its routine reply. Amber means hold the routine reply until the keeper gives a fresh instruction. A covered lantern carries no current instruction. Never borrow yesterday's meaning for a covered lantern.
A fresh instruction includes the station name and the keeper's visit number.
fresh instruction
An instruction recorded during the current station visit.
Turn the signal cards
Read the front of each card. Turn it over to check the action attached to that state. These cards teach the marsh convention; colours in other places may mean something else.
Clear opening
The opening shows an unobstructed white disc.
The next station may send its routine reply. Record clear in the route ledger.
Amber shutter
The amber panel covers half the disc.
Hold the routine reply. Wait for a fresh instruction from this visit.
Covered lantern
An opaque panel covers the whole disc.
No current instruction is visible. Ask the keeper to identify the station state.
A covered lantern
Last Reed's lantern is covered. An old ledger entry says clear. You cannot tell whether the cover is deliberate or whether the keeper has not yet started the visit.
What should you do before sending a reply?
Ask for the current station state

texts.value: Record a visit
By the end of this lesson, you can write a station entry that separates an observation from a keeper's interpretation.

Every visit entry has a station name, a visit number and the shutter state you saw. Put uncertain explanations in a separate note. "Amber at visit four" is an observation. "Perhaps the next keeper is late" is an interpretation. Both can be useful, but the next keeper must know which is which.
A visit number counts arrivals, not minutes.
visit number
A consecutive number assigned to each keeper's arrival at a station.

texts.value: Listen for spacing
By the end of this lesson, you can describe the spacing of the practice bell pattern without treating it as a station instruction.

The practice bell makes two short tones with a gap between them. The file below is a synthetic tone, not a recording from a place or a person. In Lantern Marsh, keepers use this exercise to agree on words such as short and gap before they discuss a real station bell.
A gap belongs in your description as well as the tones.
gap
The quiet interval between two tones in a bell pattern.
Hear the practice bell
Two practice tones

texts.value: Start with the record
By the end of this lesson, you can choose a first check for a loose shutter and record what that check establishes.

A shutter at Sedge Gate slips after Mira lets go. The route ledger still records amber from the previous keeper's visit. Start by observing whether the panel stays in place. Do not rewrite the old visit to make it agree with the new one. Each visit needs its own entry.
A slip check establishes position, not the reason a fastening failed.

texts.value: Choose what to carry
By the end of this lesson, you can assemble a fieldbook that supports route visits and name the limits of its instructions.

This lesson has no narration. Work at your own reading pace. Bring together your route map, signal notes and handoff entry. These pieces describe the invented west route. They do not provide rules for a real marsh, workplace or emergency.
A fieldbook helps you find the information you already checked. It cannot replace a fresh station instruction.
fieldbook
A keeper's personal collection of route sketches, signal notes and visit reminders.
Arrange your pages
Put the route sketch first so you can find the station name before recording a visit. Keep clear, amber and covered meanings together on a second page. Mark invented practice signals as practice.
Choose a handoff entry that names a visit and carries an unresolved question. Preserve any correction. Put this entry after the signal notes so you can find it during a handoff.
Try reading the fieldbook with one hand covering the page titles. If a page becomes hard to identify, add a useful label rather than more decoration.

Choose what to carry
By the end of this lesson, you can assemble a fieldbook that supports route visits and name the limits of its instructions.

This lesson has no narration. Work at your own reading pace. Bring together your route map, signal notes and handoff entry. These pieces describe the invented west route. They do not provide rules for a real marsh, workplace or emergency.
A fieldbook helps you find the information you already checked. It cannot replace a fresh station instruction.
Arrange your pages
Arrange your pages
Put the route sketch first so you can find the station name before recording a visit. Keep clear, amber and covered meanings together on a second page. Mark invented practice signals as practice.
Choose a handoff entry that names a visit and carries an unresolved question. Preserve any correction. Put this entry after the signal notes so you can find it during a handoff.
Try reading the fieldbook with one hand covering the page titles. If a page becomes hard to identify, add a useful label rather than more decoration.
